cards.heading: Definition
cards.question: What is the "selection as the bottleneck of the record" diagnosis?
cards.answer: The limit on using accumulated knowledge is not producing or storing it but consulting it — the record grows cheaply and without bound while selection is the slow, binding step.

cards.heading: Named cause
cards.question: What does the essay name as the cause of the selection bottleneck?
cards.answer: Artificial indexing — an item sits in only one place, is found only by descending from subclass to subclass, and the path rules to do so are cumbersome to learn.

cards.heading: Human recall vs. indexed filing
cards.question: How does human recall differ mechanically from indexed filing, per the essay?
cards.answer: Recall works by association — one item in mind snaps to the next along a web of trails — rather than requiring the searcher to exit the system and re-enter on a fresh path for each new item.

cards.heading: Two selection strategies
cards.question: What are the two mechanical selection strategies the essay distinguishes?
cards.answer: Simple selection, which examines every item in a set for specified characteristics, and class-narrowing selection (like an automatic telephone exchange), which attends only to a narrowing class and never touches most of the collection.

cards.heading: Why the diagnosis outlived the tech
cards.question: Why does the diagnosis still hold even though the essay's own technology (microfilm, photocells) is obsolete?
cards.answer: Every retrieval system since — catalogs, search engines, wikis — has only moved where the bottleneck sits, without dislodging the claim that consultation, not accumulation, constrains use of the record.
